artworks.title: Seduction Scene on a Terrace by Moonlight
artworks.medium: Opaque watercolor with gold on paper
artworks.curatorNote: Lean close. This moonlit terrace is a miniature painting, its image only 16.8 by 23.5 centimeters. The museum catalogues it as Mughal, from India, possibly Murshidabad in West Bengal. The record keeps the painter's name to itself, and so must we.
artworks.lesson: The plaque names the medium: opaque watercolor with gold on paper. Opaque paint covers the paper beneath it instead of letting it show through, and gold joins the watercolor on the page. The museum dates the work only to the 18th century.
artworks.alt: A small miniature painting of a terrace by moonlight, made in opaque watercolor with gold on paper.

puzzle.prompt: Which medium did the painter use for this moonlit terrace?
options: Opaque watercolor with gold on paper
puzzle.hint: The plaque describes a paint that covers the paper beneath it, and it is not oil.
puzzle.nudge: Not that one. Return to the plaque's medium line: a water-based paint, with something precious added.
puzzle.explanation: The museum record lists opaque watercolor with gold on paper for this miniature painting.

artworks.credit: Mughal, Seduction Scene on a Terrace by Moonlight, 18th century. Everett and Ann McNear Collection. Art Institute of Chicago, CC0 public domain. https://www.artic.edu/artworks/120669

artworks.title: The Girl by the Window
artworks.curatorNote: A girl in her nightgown stands in a darkened room and gazes out a window into a brighter night. Her face stays hidden from us. With one hand she draws back the pale curtain. Look down as well: moonlight lays glowing rectangles across the sharply tilted floor.
artworks.lesson: Edvard Munch painted this in 1893, the same year as The Scream. Around that time he wrote a manifesto declaring that artists should depict "living people who breathe and feel, suffer and love." Loosely applied browns, blues and greens fill the shadows, while light blues and pink whites pick out the girl and the window.
artworks.alt: A brown-haired girl in a nightgown stands in a dark room, gazing out a window into a brighter night. Her face is unseen and her hand draws back a pale curtain.

puzzle.prompt: Around the time he painted her, Munch wrote a manifesto. What kind of people did he say artists should depict?
answers: living people who breathe and feel
living people who breathe and feel, suffer and love
living people who breathe and feel suffer and love
puzzle.hint: The lesson quotes him. These people breathe and feel, suffer and love.
puzzle.nudge: Close, but the plaque used Munch's own word. Recall the quotation in the lesson and the one word that describes these people.
puzzle.explanation: Munch's manifesto called for "living people who breathe and feel, suffer and love", and this girl at the window is one of them.

artworks.credit: Edvard Munch, The Girl by the Window, 1893. Searle Family Trust and Goldabelle McComb Finn endowments; Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection. Art Institute of Chicago, CC0 public domain. https://www.artic.edu/artworks/154235

artworks.title: Pardon in Brittany
artworks.curatorNote: The title carries us to Brittany. The museum's catalogue names who and what gathers here: women and men, headdresses, a horse, and candles with a candleholder. The French painter Gaston La Touche signed the lower left corner: G. La Touche.
artworks.lesson: La Touche, who lived from 1854 to 1913, painted this in oil on canvas in 1896. The museum record links it to Chicago's Century of Progress world's fair but tells no more of its story. Where the archive falls silent, let your eyes do the reading.
artworks.alt: A gathering of women and men in headdresses in Brittany, with a horse and candles among them.

puzzle.prompt: The museum record links this canvas to a world's fair. Which one?
options: The Century of Progress in Chicago
puzzle.hint: The fair is named in the lesson, not the curator note, along with its city.
puzzle.nudge: Not that fair. The plaque named one held in the same city as the museum that owns this canvas.
puzzle.explanation: The museum record links Pardon in Brittany to Chicago's Century of Progress world's fair, as the lesson said.

artworks.credit: Gaston La Touche, Pardon in Brittany, 1896. Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection. Art Institute of Chicago, CC0 public domain. https://www.artic.edu/artworks/111656

artworks.title: Self-Portrait
artworks.curatorNote: The American painter Walter Shirlaw meets your eye in his own likeness. He left his mark at the lower right of the canvas: W. Shirlaw, 1878. The museum records no story of the sitting, so the portrait keeps its own counsel.
artworks.lesson: In a self-portrait the artist and the sitter are the same person. Shirlaw, who lived from 1838 to 1909, painted this one in oil on canvas in 1878, the year he wrote beside his name. It came to the museum as a gift of Joseph M. Rogers.
artworks.alt: A self-portrait of the painter Walter Shirlaw, signed at the lower right.

puzzle.prompt: The painter signed his name and a year on the canvas. In which corner?
puzzle.hint: The plaque tells you exactly where he left his mark, and it is not at the top.
puzzle.nudge: Not that corner. Return to the plaque's line about his name and the year.
puzzle.explanation: Shirlaw signed the lower right corner with his name and 1878, the date on the plaque.

artworks.credit: Walter Shirlaw, Self-Portrait, 1878. Gift of Joseph M. Rogers. Art Institute of Chicago, CC0 public domain. https://www.artic.edu/artworks/11

artworks.title: Approaching Storm
artworks.curatorNote: A storm creeps toward the shore. Holidaymakers wear the same clothes they would wear in the city, and they wait beside huts on wheels. Those huts were portable changing rooms, pulled into the water so bathers could change without fear of being seen.
artworks.lesson: Eugène Louis Boudin, a painter from Normandy and Claude Monet's teacher, painted this in 1864 in oil on a cradled panel. He painted in the open air, a practice Monet followed and one that mattered greatly to the painters later called the Impressionists. Boudin painted many beach scenes at the fashionable resorts of Trouville and Deauville.
artworks.alt: A beach as a storm approaches. Women in dresses and children gather beside bathing huts on wheels.

puzzle.prompt: What do the beachgoers gather beside as the storm approaches?
puzzle.hint: The plaque explains how bathers on this beach kept their modesty.
puzzle.nudge: Not those. Look for the thing the plaque says was pulled into the water.
puzzle.explanation: The museum explains that the huts on wheels were portable changing rooms, pulled into the water so bathers could change unseen.

artworks.credit: Eugène Louis Boudin, Approaching Storm, 1864. Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection. Art Institute of Chicago, CC0 public domain. https://www.artic.edu/artworks/27764

artworks.title: Fishing Boats with Hucksters Bargaining for Fish
artworks.curatorNote: J. M. W. Turner was fascinated by the sea. A crowded fishing boat rides rolling, tumultuous waves while a smaller boat of hucksters, or peddlers, draws near to bargain for fish to sell back at port. Behind them a steamship chugs along, a sign of the new industrial age.
artworks.lesson: The English painter Joseph Mallord William Turner made this large canvas in 1837 to 1838, when he was more and more drawn to atmospheric drama and the effects of light. A storm brews behind, and the sunlit water in front is dotted with thick impasto, paint laid on heavily for depth and texture. He signed it on the white flag high on the fishing boat's mast.
artworks.alt: A large marine landscape of boats on rough waves beneath storm clouds.

puzzle.prompt: The title calls the people in the smaller boat hucksters. What plainer word does the plaque give for them?
puzzle.hint: It is an everyday word for a seller of goods, and it begins with the letter P.
puzzle.nudge: Not quite. The plaque says the hucksters buy fish to sell back at port, and it gives them a second name.
puzzle.explanation: Hucksters are peddlers: they come out to buy the catch and sell it back at port.

artworks.credit: Joseph Mallord William Turner, Fishing Boats with Hucksters Bargaining for Fish, 1837–38. Mr. and Mrs. W. W. Kimball Collection. Art Institute of Chicago, CC0 public domain. https://www.artic.edu/artworks/4796
